turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell expressed her disappointment at Mr. Worthing's apparent lack of veracity and asked him to explain the discrepancy regarding his address in Belgrave Square.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that the discrepancy was due to his having inherited the house from a distant uncle and that he had not lived there himself, but had always thought of it as his home.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that his explanation was unsatisfactory and that she required a more specific account of his background and family connections.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack expressed his willingness to provide any information that would help establish his suitability as a husband for Lady Bracknell's daughter, and asked if there was any specific aspect of his background that he had not already mentioned.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell insisted that she would not consider any further explanations from Mr. Worthing until he could provide a complete and satisfactory account of his family tree, including the names of all his aunts and uncles.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack asked if it would be possible to send for the family solicitor, Mr. Shaw, who might be able to provide a detailed account of his family tree and help to clear up any uncertainty regarding his background.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing to explain why he had not mentioned Mr. Shaw, his family solicitor, earlier in their conversation, and hinted that this omission was further evidence of his dubious character.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he had not mentioned Mr. Shaw earlier because he had not been asked about his family solicitor, and he had assumed that Lady Bracknell would only be concerned with matters directly related to his relationship with Miss Gwendolen.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing that she was not interested in his speculations or assumptions, and that she would not consider his proposal to send for Mr. Shaw, the family solicitor.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told her mother that she was getting impatient and wanted to know why this was taking so long.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Gwendolen if she was quite certain she wanted to marry a man whose family history was shrouded in mystery, and whose very identity seemed to be in question.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he understood Lady Bracknell's concerns, but he could not change his circumstances, and he was willing to do his best to prove himself worthy of Miss Gwendolen's hand.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told her mother that she would not be swayed by these petty objections and that she was determined to marry Jack, no matter what.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell observed that Jack's willingness to prove himself worthy of Gwendolen's hand was a commendable sentiment, but she remained unconvinced by his dubious background.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he understood Lady Bracknell's desire for a respectable family background, but he was not ashamed of his humble upbringing, and he believed that his love for Gwendolen was a strong foundation for their marriage.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen retorted that her mother's constant questioning was beginning to wear thin and that she was starting to feel like a prize to be won in some sort of game.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that his argument about his humble upbringing being a suitable foundation for marriage was naive and misguided, and that a respectable family background was essential for a woman of Gwendolen's standing.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack asked if it would be possible for him to speak with Gwendolen, as he felt that she could vouch for his character and alleviate her mother's concerns.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told her mother that she had heard quite enough and was not going to stand idly by while her fiancé's character was being unfairly maligned.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that his request to speak with Gwendolen was absurd, as she had not yet completed her interrogation of him.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Gwendolen and Mr. Worthing to pardon her, as they were not engaged to anyone. She explained that when they did become engaged, she or Mr. Worthing's father, if his health permitted, would inform them of the fact. An engagement should come as a surprise to a young girl, and it was hardly a matter she could arrange for herself. While she was making inquiries, Gwendolen would wait for her below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen called out to Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen to wait for her in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen replied to Lady Bracknell that she would wait for her.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing to take a seat.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stood tall, his eyes locked on Lady Bracknell, and said that he preferred to remain standing, rather than take a seat.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell informed Mr. Worthing that he was not on her list of eligible young men, although she had the same list as the Duchess of Bolton. However, she was willing to enter his name if his answers were satisfactory. She asked him if he smoked.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing admitted to Lady Bracknell that he smoked.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing smoked. She believed that a man should have an occupation. There were too many idle men in London. She asked Mr. Worthing how old he was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he was twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that twenty-nine was a good age to get married. She believed that a man who wanted to get married should know either everything or nothing. She asked Mr. Worthing which category he fell into.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that he knew nothing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing knew nothing. She believed that ignorance was a delicate and exotic fruit that should not be tampered with. She stated that education was unsound and produced no effect in England. If it did, it would be a danger to the upper classes. She asked Mr. Worthing about his income.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing if his income came from land or investments.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that his income came from investments.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that Mr. Worthing's income was satisfactory. She stated that land was no longer a profit or pleasure, but rather a means of gaining position and losing it. She asked Mr. Worthing about his country house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he had a country house with some land, but he did not depend on it for his income. In fact, the poachers were the only ones who made anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing how many bedrooms his country house had. She also asked if he had a town house, as a girl like Gwendolen could not be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing who Lady Bloxham was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack observed that Lady Bracknell went out very little, and that she was a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing what number his house in Belgrave Square was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his house was number 149.
